clue.text: Just the place you might ride a Ferris wheel

definitions.text: the place you might ride a Ferris wheel

blocks.clueFragment: the place you might ride a Ferris wheel
blocks.note: second meaning: a funfair with rides and stalls

explanation.surface: Someone insists a Ferris wheel ride is the only place to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like an adverb meaning 'simply', but it is an adjective meaning impartial; the rest describes a travelling funfair.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means impartial or equitable, and is also a noun for a travelling show with rides and stalls.

clue.text: Healthy sloth possibly doesn’t stick out

blocks.note: sloth is one of the seven deadly sins; 'possibly' marks it as an example

explanation.surface: A sloth that is in good health blends into the trees rather than standing out.
explanation.walkthrough: The animal is a red herring: sloth here is the vice of laziness, one of the seven deadly sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who conforms and blends with a group is not conspicuous, the verb phrase matching 'doesn't stick out'.

clue.text: Part of meal I fed to a consumer messily

indicators.note: done messily means in disorder, so the letters end up jumbled

explanation.surface: Serving dinner to a diner who eats sloppily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fed to' attaches the letter I to the other fodder; all ten letters are then rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal dish served at dinner is one of the stages or portions of a meal.

clue.text: Get support from the French soon

blocks.note: anon is an old word for soon

explanation.surface: A promise that help from France will arrive shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the French' is a standard crossword device for LE, LA or LES; ANON is the archaic 'shortly'.
explanation.definitionFit: To rely on someone or depend upon them for help is to obtain backing from them.

clue.text: Sea creature netted in major catch

indicators.note: something netted is caught inside, so the letters sit enclosed within the following words

blocks.note: spans the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A fisherman lands a sea creature in a big haul.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of 'major' and 'catch'.
explanation.definitionFit: The killer whale is a large marine mammal, an example of a creature living in the ocean.

clue.text: 14 narcs got redeployed

indicators.note: redeployed means sent out again in a new arrangement, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Drug agents have been moved to new postings.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the answer to 14 down, GOOD FOR YOU; narcs are US drug-enforcement agents.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal exclamations offering praise or congratulation to someone on an achievement.

clue.text: One-time Quechua speaker in California

blocks.note: taken as written; that the letters also run on into the next word is a coincidence of the charade
CA is the postal abbreviation for California

explanation.surface: A speaker of an Andean language who once lived in California.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a place-word but is simply kept as written; Quechua is the language of the Andes.
explanation.definitionFit: The historic Andean empire's people spoke Quechua, so a member of it was a past speaker of that language.

clue.text: A mean dictator destroyed on South Park, perhaps

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, so the letters are smashed and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A tyrant is brutally mocked in an episode of South Park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' looks like a connector but its letters belong in the fodder; 'perhaps' marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: South Park is a long-running American television series made with drawn figures, an example of this kind of show.

clue.text: Cold alcoholic drink accompanying favourite type of airy cake

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a teacher's pet is a favourite

explanation.surface: A chilled boozy drink served alongside someone's favourite light cake.
explanation.walkthrough: A crumpet is a British griddle bread full of holes, usually toasted and buttered.
explanation.definitionFit: This spongy griddle bun is full of holes, so it can fairly be called a light, bubbly sort of teatime bake.

clue.text: Sticky substance found in sycamores, inexplicably

indicators.note: to be found in something is to be located inside it, so the letters lie within the words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A mysterious gummy secretion turns up on sycamore trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inexplicably' looks like an anagram signal, but it only lends the letters at its start.
explanation.definitionFit: The gummy secretion of trees is a classic example of a tacky, adhesive material.

clue.text: Complaint resulting from broken rule, again!

indicators.note: a broken thing has its parts out of place, so the letters must be rearranged

explanation.surface: An exasperated protest that someone has broken a rule yet again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grievance, but it is the medical sense: an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerve pain is a medical disorder, and an ailment is often called a complaint by doctors.

clue.text: Heavy rainfall starts to move over Newcastle before long

indicators.note: starts are opening letters, so only the initial of each word is kept

explanation.surface: A forecast that a downpour will shift over Newcastle shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newcastle' tempts you to use NE or a place abbreviation, but it just gives its initial along with the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The seasonal wind of South Asia brings torrential downpours, so the word is used for that wet season.

clue.text: Graduates working for someone in the building trade

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: University leavers taking jobs with a builder.
explanation.walkthrough: MA, Master of Arts, is the usual crossword graduate; its plural is MAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoneworker who cuts and lays stone or brick is a craftsman employed in construction.

clue.text: Show part of a book, then a collection of books

blocks.note: a book is made of pages
NT is the New Testament, a collection of biblical books

explanation.surface: An instruction to display a page and then a whole library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like a verb, but it is the noun; the New Testament (NT) is the crossword's usual set of books.
explanation.definitionFit: A pageant is a public spectacle or procession, a type of staged entertainment or display.

clue.text: Steak fried in butter may not be this well done

definitions.text: Steak fried in butter may not be this

blocks.clueFragment: Steak fried in butter may not be this
blocks.note: first meaning: healthy, beneficial to eat
second meaning: an exclamation of congratulation

explanation.surface: A warning that buttery steak cooked until well done is not healthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well done' looks like a cooking instruction for the steak, but it is a cry of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes something healthy to eat and is also an informal cheer of congratulation.

clue.text: Played at Holyhead regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Someone often performed at Holyhead, the Welsh ferry port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' looks like a link word, but its T is needed; start from the second letter. Holyhead is a port on Anglesey in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: To trifle or fiddle with something casually is to amuse oneself with it, the past tense matching.

clue.text: This feels ugly, or organised in a smug way

indicators.note: organised means put into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone uneasy about whether something feels ugly or merely complacently arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' looks like a connector, but its letters complete the fifteen of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with a sanctimonious sense of moral superiority is behaving complacently pleased with oneself.

clue.text: Place for a case?

blocks.note: surface reading: somewhere to keep a suitcase or box
setter's reading: a legal case, heard before a judge

explanation.walkthrough: 'case' first suggests a container or luggage; the question mark points to a lawsuit instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal disputes are heard in a building where judges sit, so that is the venue for a lawsuit.

clue.text: Island nation’s unstable danger area

indicators.note: unstable means liable to shift, so the letters do not stay in order

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A country with a volatile zone of peril.
explanation.walkthrough: '’s' stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenada is a sovereign country in the Caribbean consisting of one main island and smaller ones.

clue.text: Presently present, or completely absent?

definitions.note: an adjective phrase; the answer is used predicatively, as in 'he was nowhere'

explanation.surface: A riddle: is someone currently in attendance, or not there at all?
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer and it means the opposite of the whole: now here versus nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not in any place at all is entirely missing, so the word serves for utter absence.

clue.text: Jointly start puzzle that’s missing its first number?

indicators.note: missing means lacking, and 'its first' says the earliest occurrence is the one dropped

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: Starting a crossword together that turns out to lack clue one.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb has two Ns; only the first one goes.
explanation.definitionFit: To establish an organisation together with a partner is to set it up alongside someone else.

clue.text: Two-bit firm securing great deal

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so one piece wraps around another

explanation.surface: A tinpot company landing a big contract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great deal' reads as a contract, but it means a large amount.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal adjectives meaning inexpensive, shoddy or of little worth.

clue.text: Fuddy-duddy relative almost about to go, finally

definitions.note: used here as an adjective, old-fashioned

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
finally points to the end, so only the closing letters are kept
about means around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: last letter of each of the two words

explanation.surface: A stuffy old uncle nearly ready to leave at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' applies to both 'to' and 'go', giving two Os.
explanation.definitionFit: A fuddy-duddy is a fogey, someone unfashionable and conservative, so as an adjective it means not trendy.

clue.text: Pass on report of decent attendance on match day

indicators.note: a report is something spoken and heard, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: proper means decent; the gate is the number of spectators at a game

explanation.surface: Relaying news that a good crowd turned up for the game.
explanation.walkthrough: In British sport the 'gate' is the attendance at a match; said in a non-rhotic accent, 'proper gate' matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To spread or transmit something, such as an idea or a gene, to others is to hand it along.

clue.text: Rubbish American party’s leader broadcast on the radio?

definitions.text: party’s leader broadcast on the radio?

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Dismissing a US party chief's radio address as nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the letter P, the leader of 'party', as said in the radio alphabet; 'American party' wants to be one unit but must split.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO phonetic alphabet used by radio operators, the letter P is spoken as this code word.

clue.text: Declare a very obvious willingness at the outset

indicators.note: the outset is the beginning, so each word gives its opening letter

explanation.surface: Stating plainly, right from the start, that you are eager to help.
explanation.walkthrough: Four words give four initials.
explanation.definitionFit: To avow is to state openly or assert something, a formal synonym for announcing or affirming.

clue.text: Extremely readable and better summary

indicators.note: extremes are the two ends, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: to cap a story is to better it

explanation.surface: Praise for a digest that is very easy to read and improved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for 'readable' but takes its ends; 'better' is a verb meaning outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: A recap, short for recapitulation, is a brief restatement of the main points, an informal synonym.

clue.text: Group of whales crossing northern body of water

indicators.note: crossing means spanning, so one piece stretches across and around another

blocks.note: a pod is a school of whales
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A school of whales swimming across a northern sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' looks like travel, but it is the instruction to put one piece around the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pool of standing water is one kind of lake-like expanse, a modest example of the category.

clue.text: What she is is also what he is?

definitions.text: What she is is also what he is?

blocks.clueFragment: What she is is also what he is?
blocks.note: surface reading: a woman and a man share some quality or job
setter's reading: the words 'she' and 'he' themselves, as parts of speech

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a remark about equality between two people; instead it asks what grammatical class the two words belong to.
explanation.definitionFit: Words such as I, you, he and she stand in for people in grammar, forming the same word class.
